title: Trivial closed fibre detects a trivial closed subgroup of a split torus
statement: Let $(A,\mathfrak m)$ be a commutative Noetherian local ring [def-weil-pbc-noetherian-ring], put $k=A/\mathfrak m$ and $S=\operatorname{Spec}A$ [def-weil-affine-spectrum], and let $r\geq0$. An $S$-group scheme is an $S$-scheme with multiplication, identity section and inverse satisfying the associativity, unit and inverse diagrams; a homomorphism preserves these three operations. Let $T=\operatorname{Spec}A[x_1,y_1,\ldots,x_r,y_r]/(x_iy_i-1)_{1\leq i\leq r}$, with $\Delta(x_i)=x_i\otimes x_i$, $\Delta(y_i)=y_i\otimes y_i$, counit $x_i,y_i\mapsto1$ and inverse interchanging $x_i,y_i$; for $r=0$, $T=1_S$. Let $j:K\hookrightarrow T$ be a closed immersion [def-weil-closed-immersion] of $S$-group schemes which is a homomorphism. If the identity section $\operatorname{Spec}k\to K_k=K\times_S\operatorname{Spec}k$ [def-pc-base-change] is an isomorphism, then the identity section $S\to K$ is an isomorphism. Neither flatness of $K\to S$ nor completeness of $A$ is assumed.

source.place: Conrad, Reductive group schemes (2014), Exercise 2.4.3(iii), printed p.76, the trivial-special-fibre kernel argument, extracted for an arbitrary closed subgroup of a split torus; also the final torsion argument in the proof of Theorem B.3.2(2), printed pp.289-290. Agent-extracted supporting statement, not a verbatim theorem of the source. WANTED local archive; online source read.

proof.text: Write $P=A[x_1,y_1,\ldots,x_r,y_r]/(x_iy_i-1)$. The affine description of a closed immersion gives $K=\operatorname{Spec}B$, with $B=P/I$. The identity section gives an augmentation $\epsilon:B\to A$ sending every $x_i,y_i$ to $1$. Its composite with the structure map $u:A\to B$ is $1_A$, so $B=u(A)\oplus J$ as $A$-modules, where $J=\ker\epsilon$. The ideal $J$ is generated as a $B$-module by the $2r$ elements $x_i-1,y_i-1$: subtracting the value at $(1,\ldots,1)$ from a polynomial is a sum of multiples of these differences, and this passes to $B$. In particular $J$ is finite as a $B$-module, even though $B$ need not be finite as an $A$-module. For $r=0$ the same description already gives $J=0$.

source.place: Exercise 2.4.3(iii), printed p.76; affine augmentation setup written out by Q98

proof.text: For an integer $n>1$, let $H_n=\ker([n]:K\to K)$. Its functor of points consists of tuples in $K$ whose coordinates have $n$th power $1$. Thus $H_n=\operatorname{Spec}C_n$ with $C_n=B/(x_i^n-1,y_i^n-1)_i$. Since $x_iy_i=1$, the second family of relations follows from the first and $y_i=x_i^{n-1}$ in $C_n$. Consequently the finitely many monomials $\prod_i x_i^{a_i}$ with $0\leq a_i<n$ span $C_n$ over $A$. The augmentation splits $C_n=A\oplus L_n$, where $L_n$ is its augmentation kernel; $L_n$ is a finite $A$-module, being the image of the finite module $C_n$ under $c\mapsto c-u\epsilon(c)$. The affine fibre-product formula and the hypothesis identify $C_n/\mathfrak mC_n$ with $k$: indeed $(H_n)_k=\ker([n]:K_k\to K_k)=1_k$. Reduction of the split decomposition gives $L_n/\mathfrak mL_n=0$. Since $\mathfrak m$ is the Jacobson radical of $A$, Nakayama gives $L_n=0$. Hence $H_n=1_S$ for every $n>1$.

source.place: Exercise 2.4.3(iii), printed p.76; Theorem B.3.2(2), final torsion paragraph, printed pp.289-290; Nakayama: Stacks 00DV (lemma-NAK)(2)

proof.text: Fix a prime $\mathfrak p\subset A$, put $F=\kappa(\mathfrak p)$, and choose an algebraic closure $\Omega/F$. Base change of the closed immersion embeds $K_\Omega$ as a closed subgroup of $\mathbf G_{m,\Omega}^r$. The cited subgroup theorem gives $K_\Omega\simeq D_\Omega(M)$ for a finitely generated abelian group $M$. The group-algebra basis in its statement computes the coordinate algebra of $D_\Omega(M)[n]$ as $\Omega[M]/(e_{nm}-1:m\in M)=\Omega[M/nM]$: the quotient map sends $e_m$ to $e_{\bar m}$, and the inverse sends a coset basis vector to the class of any representative; representatives differing by $nm'$ give the same class. From Step 2 these torsion schemes are trivial. Thus $M/nM=0$ for every $n>1$, because the augmentation of $\Omega[M/nM]$ is an isomorphism only when its basis has just the identity index. By the structure theorem for finitely generated abelian groups, a nonzero free summand has a nonzero quotient modulo $2$, and any nonzero cyclic prime-power summand has a nonzero quotient modulo its prime. Therefore $M=0$ and $K_\Omega=1_\Omega$. This uses scheme-theoretic torsion, including $p$-power torsion in characteristic $p$, rather than just geometric points.

source.place: Exercise 2.4.3(iii), printed p.76; final torsion argument of Theorem B.3.2(2), printed pp.289-290; diagonalizable subgroup input also Milne Theorems 12.8-12.9, pp.233-234

proof.text: Let $B_F=B\otimes_A F$. Its augmentation to $F$ becomes an isomorphism after scalar extension to $\Omega$, by Step 3 and the affine fibre-product formula. If $b\in B_F$ has augmentation zero, its image in $B_F\otimes_F\Omega$ is zero; the cited field-extension injection gives $b=0$. The augmentation is already surjective since it has its scalar section. Hence $B_F\simeq F$ by the augmentation itself. Tensoring the split decomposition $B=A\oplus J$ gives $B_F=F\oplus(J\otimes_A F)$ (send $(a,j)\otimes t$ to $(at,j\otimes t)$ and use the two inclusions for the inverse), so $J\otimes_A\kappa(\mathfrak p)=0$ for every prime $\mathfrak p\subset A$.

source.place: Exercise 2.4.3(iii), printed p.76, passage from geometric to ordinary fibres; Q98 affine form of the final fibre argument

proof.text: For any prime $\mathfrak q\subset B$, put $\mathfrak p=u^{-1}(\mathfrak q)$ and $S_{\mathfrak p}=A\setminus\mathfrak p$. Write $S_{\mathfrak p}^{-1}J$ for module localization. The maps $j\otimes(\bar a/\bar s)\mapsto (aj/s)\bmod\mathfrak pS_{\mathfrak p}^{-1}J$ and $j/s\mapsto j\otimes(1/\bar s)$ identify $J\otimes_A\kappa(\mathfrak p)$ with $S_{\mathfrak p}^{-1}J/\mathfrak pS_{\mathfrak p}^{-1}J$; the fraction relation and balancing check that both are well defined and inverse. Step 4 therefore implies that every $j/1$ is a finite sum of terms $(a/1)(j'/s)$ with $a\in\mathfrak p$. All $u(s)$ are invertible in $B_{\mathfrak q}$. Thus $J_{\mathfrak q}=\mathfrak pJ_{\mathfrak q}$, where $J_{\mathfrak q}$ denotes the localization of the $B$-module $J$. It is finite over the local ring $B_{\mathfrak q}$ by the generators in Step 1, and the ideal generated by $u(\mathfrak p)$ is contained in its maximal ideal $\mathfrak qB_{\mathfrak q}$. Nakayama over $B_{\mathfrak q}$ yields $J_{\mathfrak q}=0$.

source.place: Tag 00DV (lemma-NAK)(2); localization and residue-field definitions (00CO, 07BI); Q98 affine specialization of Conrad Lemma B.3.1 for an identity section

proof.text: Finally let $j\in J$. Since $j/1=0$ in every $J_{\mathfrak q}$, the localization zero criterion says that for each prime $\mathfrak q\subset B$ there exists $s\notin\mathfrak q$ with $sj=0$. If $j\ne0$, its annihilator would be a proper ideal, hence contained in a maximal ideal $\mathfrak q$ (apply Zorn to proper ideals containing it: a chain union is proper because it does not contain $1$). The preceding $s$ would belong to this annihilator and lie outside $\mathfrak q$, a contradiction. Therefore $J=0$ and the augmentation $B\to A$ is inverse to $u$. Taking spectra proves that the actual identity section $S\to K$ is an isomorphism. No step assumed flatness of $K$ or completeness of $A$.

source.place: Localization zero criterion, Section 00CM; elementary annihilator argument completing the affine fibre argument
